title: A fixed number
translation: People know the word jōgaku, "fixed number", from temple monks: certain temples have a fixed number of official monks. But it isn't only used for monks. The Engishiki also has "jōgaku palace women". It's the general word for any public post with a set number of people.
original: {諸寺|しよじ}の{僧|そう}のみにもあらず、{定額|ぢやうがく}の{女嬬|によじゆ}といふこと、{延喜式|えんぎしき}に{見|み}えたり。
すべて{数|かず}さだまりたる{公人|くにん}の{通号|つうがう}にこそ。
literal: It is not only (said of) the monks of the various temples: the expression 'fixed-number nyoju' appears in the Engishiki.
It is surely the common name for public servants whose number is fixed.

notes.quote: 諸寺の僧のみにもあらず
notes.text: The sentence starts in the middle of a thought: the word it is about, {定額|ぢやうがく}, only comes in the next phrase. Readers knew it from {定額僧|ぢやうがくそう}, the monks appointed in a fixed number to officially recognised temples. The translation puts that fact first.
{女嬬|によじゆ}: low-ranking women serving in the palace. The 1925 edition glosses the phrase as 'a fixed number of low-ranking women officials'.

The Engishiki, a large collection of detailed rules for government offices and court rites, begun in the Engi era and completed in 927. The 1925 edition describes it as a book of yearly ceremonies, compiled by Fujiwara no Tokihira and Fujiwara no Tadahira.
{公人|くにん}: anyone in public service, from officials down to palace staff. {通号|つうがう}: a general name that covers many cases.
こそ with no verb after it: the rest ('it is') is left out. Compare section 180.
